title: The Lore Behind Edgar Allan Poe

shots.line: On October 3rd, 1849, a man was found slumped outside a tavern in Baltimore.
shots.scene: Neon Baltimore street at night, Poe slumped; chaos camera

shots.line: It was election day.
shots.scene: Tavern used as a polling place; voters stream in

shots.line: He was delirious, he couldn't explain where he'd been, and he was wearing someone else's clothes.
shots.scene: Poe spins in someone else's clothes amid staring eyes

shots.line: He had been missing for five days.
Four days later, he was dead.
shots.scene: A graveyard under a bone-white moon

shots.line: His name was Edgar Allan Poe.
shots.scene: Kaleidoscope of Poe faces around his bust

shots.line: He invented the detective story.

params.title: THE MURDERS IN THE RUE MORGUE

shots.line: And he left behind the one mystery nobody has ever solved.
shots.scene: An endless corridor of doors; Poe walks into it

shots.line: This is the lore behind Edgar Allan Poe.
He was born in Boston in 1809, to a family of traveling actors.
shots.scene: A stage with curtains; two actors perform

shots.line: His father walked out when he was a baby.
When Edgar was two, his mother died of tuberculosis in a rented room in Richmond, Virginia.
shots.scene: A dim rented room; the mother fades

shots.line: A wealthy tobacco merchant named John Allan and his wife Frances took the boy in.
shots.scene: John and Frances Allan take him in; coins rain

shots.line: They never formally adopted him.
But they gave him a home, an education, and a new middle name.
shots.scene: A home, an education, a new name

shots.line: Allan. A-L-L-A-N.
Not Allen.
That middle name is the only thing of John Allan's that Poe would keep.
shots.scene: Poe and John Allan, back to back

shots.line: Because the two of them hated each other.
John Allan wanted a businessman.
Edgar wanted to be a poet.
shots.scene: Edgar wanted to be a poet

shots.line: When Poe went to the University of Virginia, Allan sent him barely enough money to survive.
shots.scene: University of Virginia: Poe at a desk, barely any money

shots.line: So Poe gambled to cover the difference, and lost.
He left after one year, buried in debt, and Allan refused to pay it.
At eighteen, broke and furious, Poe did something strange.
He joined the United States Army under a fake name: Edgar A. Perry.
shots.scene: Soldiers marching; Poe enlists under a fake name

shots.line: That same year, he published his first book of poems.
It didn't say Edgar Allan Poe on the cover.
It said, "by a Bostonian."
Almost nobody bought it.
He made it to West Point.
Then, when John Allan finally cut him off for good, Poe got himself thrown out on purpose.
shots.scene: John Allan turns away for good

shots.line: He simply stopped showing up to class, to drills,
to church, until the academy had no choice but to expel him.
He was twenty-two, with no money, no family, and no name.
shots.scene: Alone: no money, no family, no name

shots.line: All he had was his writing.
shots.scene: All he had was his writing

shots.line: In Baltimore, he moved in with his aunt, Maria Clemm, and her young daughter, Virginia.
shots.scene: Baltimore street; aunt Maria and young Virginia

shots.line: In 1836, Poe married Virginia.
He was twenty-seven.
She was thirteen.
On the marriage bond, her age was listed as twenty-one.
shots.scene: The marriage bond: age listed as 21

shots.line: They were desperately poor.
Poe worked as an editor, wrote reviews, and made enemies everywhere with his vicious criticism.
shots.scene: Editor and vicious critic; enemies gather

shots.line: And in between, he wrote stories nobody had ever written before.
shots.scene: Stories nobody had written: eyes kaleidoscope

shots.line: In 1841, he published "The Murders in the Rue Morgue."
shots.scene: The Murders in the Rue Morgue, 1841

params.title: THE MURDERS IN THE RUE MORGUE

shots.line: A brilliant amateur named Dupin solves an impossible crime using nothing but logic.
It's widely considered the first modern detective story.
Decades later, Arthur Conan Doyle would admit that Sherlock Holmes owed everything to Dupin.
shots.scene: Sherlock Holmes owed everything to Dupin

shots.line: Poe wrote about premature burial, about a man walled up alive,
about a murderer driven mad by the sound of his victim's heart, still beating beneath the floorboards.
shots.scene: The tell-tale heart beating under the floorboards

shots.line: Where did all that darkness come from?
shots.scene: Where did the darkness come from? corridor

shots.line: Some of it came from home.
In 1842, Virginia was singing for friends when she began to cough up blood.
It was tuberculosis,
the same disease that had killed Poe's mother.
shots.scene: The same disease that killed Poe's mother

shots.line: For five years, she got better, then worse, then better again.
And Poe watched it happen.
In January 1845,
he published a poem about a grieving man visited by a raven that will only say one word.
shots.scene: The pendulum hall; a raven sweeps through

shots.line: "The Raven" made Edgar Allan Poe famous overnight.
It was reprinted across the country.
People recited it in theaters.
Strangers called him "The Raven" in the street.
shots.scene: Strangers call him "The Raven" in the street

shots.line: He was reportedly paid about nine dollars for it.
Fame didn't make him rich.
And it couldn't save Virginia.
In January 1847, in a freezing cottage outside New York, she died.
She was twenty-four.
They were so poor that, as she lay dying, her husband's old military coat served as her blanket.
shots.scene: His old army coat as her blanket

shots.line: After Virginia's death, Poe fell apart. He drank. He traveled.
He proposed to more than one woman.
And in 1849, he went back to Richmond
and found his childhood sweetheart, Elmira Shelton, now a widow. They became engaged.
For a moment, it looked like Edgar Allan Poe might get a happy ending.
On September 27th, 1849, he left Richmond by boat,
heading north on business, planning to come back and marry her.
He never arrived.
For five days, nobody knows where he was.
shots.scene: Five lost days: the corridor of doors

shots.line: Then, on October 3rd,
a printer named Joseph Walker found him outside a Baltimore tavern that was being used as a polling place.
shots.scene: Joseph Walker finds Poe outside the polling-place tavern

shots.line: Walker wrote to one of Poe's acquaintances that the poet was in great distress, and needed immediate help.

params.title: BALTIMORE CITY, OCT. 3RD
params.body: "...in great distress... in need of immediate assistance."

shots.line: Poe was taken to a hospital.
For four days, he drifted in and out of delirium, hallucinating, talking to things that weren't there.
shots.scene: Delirium: a vortex of staring eyes

shots.line: According to his doctor, on his last night, he called out a name, over and over: "Reynolds."
Nobody knows who Reynolds was.
On October 7th, 1849, Edgar Allan Poe died. He was forty years old.
His death certificate has never been found.
So what killed him?
The most famous theory is called cooping.
In nineteenth-century Baltimore, gangs would kidnap strangers on election day, get them drunk,
shots.scene: Election-day gangs grab strangers and get them drunk

shots.line: change their clothes, and drag them from polling place to polling place to vote again and again.
shots.scene: Dragged from polling place to polling place

shots.line: Poe was found at a polling place, on election day, in clothes that weren't his.
shots.scene: Polling place, election day, not his clothes

shots.line: But there are other theories. Alcohol.
A beating. A brain tumor. Carbon monoxide. Flu.
shots.scene: A beating, a tumor, carbon monoxide, flu

shots.line: In 1996, a doctor reviewing his symptoms argued that Poe died of rabies.
None of them can be proven.
And then the lore gets even darker.
Because after Poe died, his reputation was murdered too.
A rival editor named Rufus Griswold, a man Poe had once criticized, published an obituary that began:
"Edgar Allan Poe is dead.
This announcement will startle many, but few will be grieved by it."

params.title: DEATH OF EDGAR A. POE
params.body: "Edgar Allan Poe is dead. This announcement will startle many, but few will be grieved by it."

shots.line: Then Griswold somehow became Poe's literary executor.
shots.scene: Griswold, literary executor, holding the papers

shots.line: He wrote a biography that painted Poe as a drunk, a madman,
and a man without friends, and he forged letters to prove it.
It backfired.
Griswold's lies made Poe sound exactly like one of his own characters. The tortured genius. The madman in the dark.
shots.scene: The tortured genius, the madman in the dark

shots.line: And readers couldn't get enough.
The legend kept growing, even at his grave.
For sixty years, from 1949 to 2009, every year on Poe's birthday,
a mysterious figure dressed in black slipped into the cemetery in Baltimore
shots.scene: A figure in black slips into the cemetery

shots.line: and left three roses and a half-empty bottle of cognac.
shots.scene: Three roses and cognac on the grave

shots.line: People staked out the grave for decades.
Nobody ever unmasked the Poe Toaster.
So here's the lore of Edgar Allan Poe.
shots.scene: Here's the lore of Edgar Allan Poe

shots.line: An orphan who took his name from a man who rejected him.
A poet who sold his most famous poem for almost nothing.
shots.scene: A poem sold for almost nothing

shots.line: A husband who lost everyone he loved to the same disease.
A man who invented the detective story, and
then disappeared into a mystery that the greatest detectives in history still can't solve. Quoth the raven:
shots.scene: Falling into the spiral staircase; QUOTH THE RAVEN

shots.line: nevermore.
